_comment: Agronomic recommendation mappings. Disease treatment + growth monitoring keyed by Component 2 class name; fertilizer rules keyed by Component 4 soil health class plus nutrient thresholds.

Healthy.summary: No disease detected. The leaf shows normal colour, shape and surface texture.
Healthy.immediate_action: No treatment required. Continue the routine crop care schedule.
organic_control: Keep applying neem oil spray once every 14 days as a preventive measure
Maintain field sanitation — remove fallen leaves and weeds around the plants
chemical_control: No chemical application needed at this stage
cultural_practice: Maintain 45-60 cm spacing between plants for good air movement
Irrigate at the base of the plant, avoid wetting the foliage
Scout the field twice a week for early symptoms

Leaf Curl.summary: Upward or downward curling of leaves, usually caused by chilli leaf curl virus spread by whitefly, or by thrips and mite feeding damage.
Leaf Curl.immediate_action: Uproot and destroy severely infected plants — the virus cannot be cured once inside the plant. Control the insect vector immediately to stop further spread.
organic_control: Spray neem oil at 5 ml per litre of water, repeat every 7 days for 3 rounds
Install yellow sticky traps at 10-12 traps per acre to catch whitefly and thrips
Spray a garlic and chilli extract as a repellent between neem rounds
chemical_control: Imidacloprid 17.8 SL at 0.3 ml per litre against whitefly
Spiromesifen 22.9 SC at 1 ml per litre against mites and thrips
Rotate the insecticide group every spray to avoid resistance build-up
cultural_practice: Remove and burn infected plants away from the field, do not compost them
Grow a maize or sorghum barrier crop around the chilli block
Control weeds such as Parthenium that host the virus
Use virus-tolerant chilli varieties in the next planting cycle

Leaf Spot.summary: Circular brown or grey spots with dark margins, typically Cercospora leaf spot or bacterial leaf spot. Spreads fast in wet, humid weather.
Leaf Spot.immediate_action: Remove and destroy affected leaves, then apply a protective fungicide before the next rain.
organic_control: Spray Bordeaux mixture at 1 percent, or copper oxychloride at 3 g per litre
Apply Trichoderma viride or Pseudomonas fluorescens as a foliar spray at 5 g per litre
Spray diluted buttermilk or a baking soda solution as a mild surface treatment
chemical_control: Mancozeb 75 WP at 2.5 g per litre, repeat after 10-12 days
Carbendazim 50 WP at 1 g per litre for persistent infection
Alternate the two so the pathogen does not develop resistance
cultural_practice: Avoid overhead irrigation — switch to drip or furrow watering
Improve drainage so water does not stand between rows
Do not work in the field while the plants are wet
Follow a 2-year crop rotation with a non-solanaceous crop

Whitefly.summary: Whitefly infestation. Tiny white insects on the leaf underside sucking sap, leaving sticky honeydew and sooty mould. They are also the vector for leaf curl virus.
Whitefly.immediate_action: Start vector control at once. Whitefly damage is secondary — the real risk is virus transmission across the whole block.
organic_control: Spray neem oil at 5 ml per litre on the underside of leaves, every 5-7 days
Install yellow sticky traps at 12-15 per acre at canopy height
Release Encarsia formosa parasitoid wasps if available locally
Spray insecticidal soap at 10 ml per litre in the early morning
chemical_control: Imidacloprid 17.8 SL at 0.3 ml per litre as a foliar spray
Diafenthiuron 50 WP at 1.2 g per litre for heavy infestation
Spray in the early morning or late evening when whitefly are least active
cultural_practice: Remove weeds and volunteer plants that harbour whitefly populations
Use silver reflective mulch between rows to repel incoming adults
Avoid excess nitrogen — soft, lush growth attracts whitefly
Inspect the underside of leaves twice a week

Yellowish.summary: Yellowing of the leaves (chlorosis). Usually a nitrogen or magnesium deficiency, waterlogged roots, or the early stage of a viral infection.
Yellowish.immediate_action: Check root-zone drainage first, then correct the nutrient deficiency with a foliar feed for a fast response.
organic_control: Apply well-decomposed compost or farmyard manure at 2-3 kg per plant
Spray 1 percent Epsom salt solution if the yellowing is between the leaf veins
Drench with vermicompost tea once a week to improve nutrient uptake
chemical_control: Foliar spray of urea at 2 percent for a quick nitrogen correction
Spray 19:19:19 water-soluble fertilizer at 5 g per litre
Apply a micronutrient mixture containing Fe, Zn and Mg at 2 g per litre
cultural_practice: Improve drainage — waterlogging is the most common cause of chilli yellowing
Check soil pH; nutrients lock up outside the 6.0-7.0 range
Loosen compacted soil around the root zone
If yellowing is patchy and mosaic-like, suspect virus and isolate the plant

Anthracnose.summary: Anthracnose (fruit rot / die-back) caused by Colletotrichum. Sunken dark lesions with concentric rings on fruit and leaves. It is the most damaging chilli disease in wet season conditions.
Anthracnose.immediate_action: Remove and destroy all infected fruit and shoots immediately, then begin a systemic fungicide programme. Do not delay — losses escalate quickly once fruiting starts.
organic_control: Spray Trichoderma harzianum at 5 g per litre every 10 days
Apply copper oxychloride at 3 g per litre as a protective cover spray
Treat seeds with hot water at 52 deg C for 30 minutes before the next sowing
chemical_control: Azoxystrobin 23 SC at 1 ml per litre, the most effective option for anthracnose
Difenoconazole 25 EC at 0.5 ml per litre as an alternate spray
Chlorothalonil 75 WP at 2 g per litre as a protective barrier before rain
Repeat every 10-12 days through the fruiting stage
cultural_practice: Harvest ripe fruit promptly — over-ripe fruit on the plant spreads spores
Destroy all crop residue after harvest, do not leave it in the field
Stake the plants so fruit does not touch the soil
Practise a 3-year rotation away from chilli, tomato and brinjal

Healthy.canopy_condition: Full canopy, uniform green colour, normal leaf expansion
Healthy.recovery_outlook: Plant is developing on schedule. No intervention needed.
watch_for: Any new yellowing or curling on the growing tips
White insects on the underside of leaves
Spotting after periods of heavy rain

Leaf Curl.expected_yield_impact: Heavy loss — 50 to 80 percent if the infection spreads
Leaf Curl.canopy_condition: Leaves curled and reduced in size, shortened internodes, bushy stunted appearance
Leaf Curl.recovery_outlook: Infected plants will not recover. Focus on protecting the remaining healthy plants from the vector.
watch_for: Curling appearing on neighbouring plants — indicates active spread
Whitefly population on nearby healthy plants
Flower drop and failure to set fruit

Leaf Spot.expected_yield_impact: Moderate loss — 20 to 35 percent if left untreated
Leaf Spot.canopy_condition: Spotted leaves, progressive defoliation from the lower canopy upward
Leaf Spot.recovery_outlook: Good recovery expected if treated within a week. New growth should emerge clean.
watch_for: Spots spreading to the upper canopy
Rate of leaf drop after each rain event
Spots appearing on the fruit surface

Whitefly.expected_yield_impact: High risk — 30 to 60 percent, mainly through virus transmission
Whitefly.canopy_condition: Sap loss causing weak growth, sticky honeydew and black sooty mould on leaf surfaces
Whitefly.recovery_outlook: Plant recovers well once the population is controlled, provided no virus has been transmitted.
watch_for: Leaf curl symptoms appearing 10-15 days after infestation
Sooty mould reducing the photosynthetic leaf area
Adult whitefly clouds rising when plants are disturbed

Yellowish.expected_yield_impact: Moderate loss — 15 to 30 percent if the deficiency continues
Yellowish.canopy_condition: Pale to yellow foliage, thin canopy, reduced new shoot growth
Yellowish.recovery_outlook: Quick recovery, often within 10-14 days, once the deficiency or drainage problem is corrected.
watch_for: Whether the new growth comes out green after feeding
Yellowing pattern — whole leaf points to nitrogen, between veins points to magnesium
Standing water around the root zone after irrigation

Anthracnose.expected_yield_impact: Severe loss — 60 to 90 percent of marketable fruit
Anthracnose.canopy_condition: Shoot die-back, defoliation, sunken lesions on fruit making it unmarketable
Anthracnose.recovery_outlook: Existing infected fruit cannot be saved. Aggressive treatment can protect the later flushes.
watch_for: New lesions on green fruit — the earliest sign of the next infection wave
Spore spread after every rainfall or overhead irrigation

ph_bands.label: Strongly Acidic
ph_bands.advice: Apply agricultural lime or dolomite at 500-1000 kg per hectare, 3-4 weeks before planting. Below pH 5.5 phosphorus and molybdenum become locked and unavailable to the crop.

ph_bands.label: Slightly Acidic
ph_bands.advice: Apply dolomite at 250-500 kg per hectare to lift the pH toward 6.5. Dolomite also supplies magnesium, which chilli responds well to.

ph_bands.label: Optimal
ph_bands.advice: The pH is in the ideal 6.0-7.5 range for chilli. No correction needed — nutrient availability is at its best here.

ph_bands.label: Alkaline
ph_bands.advice: Apply elemental sulphur at 200-400 kg per hectare, or gypsum on sodic soils. Above pH 7.5 iron and zinc become deficient, so add a chelated micronutrient spray.

Low.dose: Apply 130-150 kg per hectare, split into 3 doses
Low.note: Split at planting, 30 days and 60 days. Nitrogen leaches quickly in the wet zone, so never apply the full quantity in one go.

Optimal.dose: Maintenance dose of 60-80 kg per hectare
Optimal.note: Nitrogen is in the right range. Apply only a light top dressing at the flowering stage.

High.note: Excess nitrogen produces leafy growth with poor fruit set and attracts whitefly and aphids. Let the crop draw down the surplus.

Low.dose: Apply 90-110 kg per hectare as a full basal dose
Low.note: Apply the whole quantity at land preparation and mix into the root zone. Phosphorus moves very little in soil, so surface application is wasted.

Optimal.dose: Basal dose of 50-60 kg per hectare
Optimal.note: Phosphorus is adequate. A modest basal application supports early root development.

High.note: Surplus phosphorus blocks zinc and iron uptake and runs off into waterways. Hold off until the next soil test.

Low.dose: Apply 90-110 kg per hectare, split into 2 doses
Low.note: Half at planting and half at the start of flowering. Potassium drives fruit size, pungency and colour development.

Optimal.dose: Maintenance dose of 50-60 kg per hectare
Optimal.note: Potassium is sufficient. Apply at flowering to support fruit filling.

High.note: High potassium competes with magnesium and calcium uptake, which can trigger blossom end rot in the fruit.

Healthy.headline: Maintenance Programme
Healthy.strategy: The soil is in good condition. Apply a balanced maintenance dose and focus on preserving organic matter.
Healthy.organic_matter: Apply 5-8 tonnes per hectare of well-decomposed farmyard manure or compost before the next planting.
application_schedule: Basal — full phosphorus, one third of the nitrogen and half the potassium at land preparation
30 days after planting — one third of the nitrogen
60 days after planting — remaining nitrogen and potassium at the flowering stage

Moderate.headline: Corrective Programme
Moderate.strategy: The soil needs targeted correction. Address the deficient nutrients listed below and rebuild organic matter over this season.
Moderate.organic_matter: Apply 8-12 tonnes per hectare of compost or farmyard manure, plus a green manure crop such as sunn hemp between cycles.
application_schedule: Basal — full phosphorus, one third of the nitrogen and half the potassium, plus all organic matter
20 days after planting — one third of the nitrogen with a micronutrient foliar spray
45 days after planting — remaining nitrogen and potassium
70 days after planting — foliar 19:19:19 at 5 g per litre to carry the crop through fruiting

Poor.headline: Soil Rehabilitation Programme
Poor.strategy: The soil is degraded and needs rebuilding, not just feeding. Combine heavy organic amendment with corrective fertilizer, and expect two seasons for full recovery.
Poor.organic_matter: Apply 15-20 tonnes per hectare of farmyard manure or compost. Add biochar at 2-3 tonnes per hectare if available, and incorporate a full green manure crop before replanting.
application_schedule: Pre-plant — incorporate all organic matter and any pH correction 3-4 weeks ahead of planting
Basal — full phosphorus, one quarter of the nitrogen and half the potassium
20 days after planting — one quarter of the nitrogen plus biofertilizer (Azospirillum and phosphate solubilising bacteria) at 5 kg per hectare
40 days after planting — one quarter of the nitrogen with a micronutrient mixture
65 days after planting — remaining nitrogen and potassium
Consider a legume rotation next season before returning to chilli
